name: Karlee Provenza
blurb: Karlee Provenza (Democratic, Laramie): Educator; Wyoming House District 45, 2021–Present. Unopposed in the Aug. 20, 2024 Democratic primary for State House District 45. Won the Nov. 5, 2024 general election with 62.8% of the vote.
background: Karlee Provenza was born in Pueblo, Colorado. Provenza earned a B.A. in psychology from the University of Northern Colorado in 2013, an M.A. in experimental psychology from the University of Wyoming in 2016, and a Ph.D. from the University of Wyoming in 2020. Her career experience includes working as an educator, waitress, private investigator, and professional photographer.

I grew up poor, sometimes on public assistance. In 2005, like so many other families, we lost our home to foreclosure. A year later a fire burned my grandmother's house down, my second home. With two permanently disabled parents who did everything they could to provide but weren’t able to get ahead, I knew that the deck was stacked against me. At 16 I left home and school. Through hard work, piles of student debt, and the grace of those who believed in me, I beat the odds, went to college, and earned my Ph.D. at the University of Wyoming. My obsession with justice has driven my research on the psychology of the American legal system and guided my advocacy efforts in my community. …

Many lawmakers haven’t worked hard for minimum wage, struggled to buy groceries, or gone without healthcare. But I have. While these struggles aren’t something most people put on a resume, they continue to shape how I have worked on your behalf for the past four years as your State Representative. In addition to serving as your representative, I earned my Ph.D. at the University of Wyoming in 2021 and have published and presented research across the country on how we can improve our justice system to better serve our communities. Most importantly, I have applied that knowledge to advocate for justice here in Albany County as a community organizer for justice and as a policy maker writing and voting on legislation.
education: Bachelor's: University of Northern Colorado, 2013; Ph.D: University of Wyoming, 2020; Graduate: University of Wyoming, 2016

positions.topic: Given the rise in residential property values and subsequent increase in property taxes, what tax structure changes would you support?
positions.text: In 2024, I supported a cap on how much property taxes could increase in a year and supported refunds for our hard working neighbors struggling to meet the demand of increased property taxes. I voted against property tax cuts that would hurt our public schools and were meant to benefit our wealthiest neighbors while ignoring real solutions for younger residents and those who are still paying their mortgage. I support large corporations paying their fair share of the bill in Wyoming to ensure hard working Wyomingites don’t get stuck with the brunt of our budget woes in the future. Wyoming’s boom and bust cycle hurts us all when it busts, and we need to look towards a variety of revenues that don’t put the burden on hard working people.

positions.topic: What changes to Wyoming's abortion laws would you support or oppose?
positions.text: Most people in Wyoming agree, the government should stay out of personal medical decisions that are better left to women, their families, their doctors, and their faith. Wyomingites deserve freedom from government overreach and they deserve leaders that respect our oaths to the Wyoming State Constitution which provides the right to make our own healthcare decisions. Unfortunately, extremist politicians have written laws in Wyoming that would force women to be pregnant against their will. In addition to fighting anti-choice legislation and continuing to sponsor legislation that renews our commitment to the Wyoming State Constitution, I will continue my efforts to expand birth control access so we can prevent abortion from happening at all.

positions.topic: How much authority should the legislature exert over ordinances at the city and county level?
positions.text: It is ironic that legislators complain of federal overreach and then micromanage our local governments to suit their political agendas. When deciding on whether or not to weigh in on local issues, it is important to consider what local elected officials can and cannot do. If a locally elected school board can make policies that better reflect their community, then it isn’t appropriate for legislators to dictate how they do their job. On the other hand, if a problem is presented that doesn’t fall under the powers of a local government, then it may be appropriate for the legislature to weigh in, assuming the solution fits under the Wyoming Constitution. In short, the legislature should respect local communities in solving local problems.

positions.topic: Do you support adopting an online voter registration system or automatic voter registration when applying for a Wyoming driver’s license? Why or why not?
positions.text: Absolutely! Wyoming should make voting easier for hard working communities who don’t necessarily have time during the regular workday to register or vote in-person. Creating more opportunities for voter registration online or while getting your license would allow for more people with busy lives to participate in their government while not having to juggle more errands. Allowing for these registration options would make it easier for our neighbors to request their ballot in advance, an option that encourages a more knowledgeable voter. Additionally, allowing for voter registration through these various options would remove some of the burden that we place on our County Clerks to manually register voters.

positions.topic: What is your position on backfilling losses to cities and counties if property taxes are further reduced?
positions.text: Cities and counties fund essential services like hospitals, first responders, roads, and more. If the legislature were to cut property taxes, which pay for these important services, we must find ways to pay for them so communities have roads to drive on, ambulances to call on, and teachers for our schools. Unfortunately, using a backfill option will not last long unless we raise taxes elsewhere. Cutting property taxes would be fiscally irresponsible. Instead, we should increase property tax refunds so increased property tax payments don’t harm hard working Wyomingites. Additionally, we should find more sustainable funding mechanisms like making large corporations pay their fair share for the government services they benefit from.

positions.topic: How would you prioritize capital spending/infrastructure in the state?
positions.text: Our road system is my number-one priority in terms of infrastructure. Several of our economic sectors (tourism, manufacturing, agriculture, oil and gas) are wholly or heavily dependent upon a functioning, safe and efficient road system. We have failed to adequately maintain or improve our roads for a number of years, to the point that the cost to repair and improve our road system across the state is in the hundreds of billions of dollars. I do not agree with the emphasis that the current state leadership has apparently placed on replacing or constructing new buildings around the state while ignoring our roads. I am also in support of increasing our spending on water projects around the state. Water is the lifeblood of Wyoming and we have an aging water infrastructure system that needs a large infusion of capital in order to repair, restore and enhance it.

That issue appears to have come home to roost on many of them and I think several will lose their legislative seats due to their inaction on this issue. Another local issue that was overlooked was how bad the state land office and the state land board totally dropped the ball on the proposal for the gravel pit on Coates Road. If the state land office and the governor had been doing their due diligence on this issue, they could have saved putting our community, and the proposed developer, through the turmoil and agony that has transpired. A proposal as involved and contentious as this should have never been relegated onto a ”consent list” for approval by the State Land Board. This is just another example of the complete disconnect there is between state government in Cheyenne and the rest of the state.

positions.text: Revenue / Property Taxes: My vote will always be NO to any increased taxes and I will support all reductions to Property Taxes. The Legislature is already preparing to find additional taxes to replace any reductions they give to citizens. The Legislature is discussing an increase to sales and use tax, creating an optional tax and suggesting to tax the sale of Real Estate. Oh, hell NO! K–12 Education and school choice, mental health/student well being, career and technical education, school based service programs, staff recruitment and retention are few of my interests. The Legislature really dropped the ball on not re-establishing The Wyoming Cowboy Challenge Academy for at-risk youths. The loss of the Challenge Academy has had a negative impact affecting hundreds of youth throughout the State. Seventy-five percent of the program was paid by the Wyoming National Guard, twenty-five percent by the State of Wyoming. The program helped students to graduate or earn GED Certificates, receive college scholarships and provided opportunities for technical job training. The Legislature needs to provide grants to help educate our youth about the dangers of drug and alcohol addiction and to provide additional mental health support. These are trying times and the State of Wyoming needs to be investing more into programs for the youth in our communities.

positions.topic: How would you prioritize capital spending/infrastructure in the state?
positions.text: I fully support funding on maintaining needed infrastructure for roads, bridges and highways and equipment or services required throughout the State. However, I believe we need to keep a tight rein on spending when it comes to erecting new, multimillion-dollar buildings with chandeliers that cost tens of thousands of dollars at a time when the State can’t support needed services for its citizens. What is a state issue that you think is overlooked? Appropriation and a review of integrity and fairness in gaming. While gaming has become a billion-dollar-a-year industry in our State, helping to fill coffers, we can no longer walk into an establishment that isn’t packed full of slot machines. In communities already struggling to deal with alcohol and drug abuse, we have now added minimally regulated gambling. This issue has been overlooked by our Legislature and needs to be addressed expeditiously.

positions.topic: What can the Legislature do to improve public health?
positions.text: Wyoming is eight years behind the curve on approving Medicaid Expansion. The bill passed the House of Representatives last session, but not the Senate. The State of Wyoming has lost millions and millions of dollars, resulting in an increasingly negative impact on our citizens, physicians and hospitals across the State by continuing not to come to terms with the issues surrounding the need for services these funds could provide. Nearly all states throughout the United States report a very positive impact after approving Medicaid expansion in their states. Local counties and the State of Wyoming should be working in collaboration with our hospitals on their needs to provide excellent care to our communities. Grants need to be established and in-depth discussions need to be happening. As a State Senator I will work to maintain a constant, open line of communication with our hospitals and their administrations. Healthcare Education and the welfare of Wyoming citizens is important for business development and the retention of our citizens. Please everyone make your vote count and vote in the Primary Election August 20, 2024. name: Tami Young
blurb: Tami Young (Republican, Worland): Co-owner, with her husband, of Young’s Camper Repair in Worland (launched 2020); also described on her campaign site as working part-time as an orthodontist assistant and as an Emotion Code, Body Code, and Belief Code practitioner. Lost the Aug. 20, 2024 Republican primary for State House District 27 with 37.0% of the vote.
occupation: Co-owner, with her husband, of Young’s Camper Repair in Worland (launched 2020); also described on her campaign site as working part-time as an orthodontist assistant and as an Emotion Code, Body Code, and Belief Code practitioner
background: Describes six-generation Wyoming roots to early settlers of Crystal Creek north of Greybull. Grew up in Worland, later graduated from Kelly Walsh High School after her family moved to Casper, and returned to Worland in 2009 after a 2009 divorce, later marrying her husband, Tim; together they have eight children. Her campaign biography also says she previously taught English grammar at Provo High School through Utah Valley University, worked as a photographer, is fluent in Spanish, and has served in the Washakie County GOP as precinct committee member, state committeewoman, and chairman, with more than 13 years in local Republican Party work.
education: Graduated from Kelly Walsh High School in Casper. Associate’s degree in photography; bachelor’s degree from Brigham Young University with a focus on marriage and family therapy (her campaign site called it a Bachelor of Science; a 2024 Basin Republican Rustler candidate profile said a bachelor’s “with an emphasis in social services and marriage and family therapy”). Between the two degrees she served a year-and-a-half church mission in Argentina.

positions.topic: Core values
positions.text: In a candidate-submitted Rustler profile she said her core values are “freedom, life, the Second Amendment, family, minimal government spending, low taxes, and small government,” and that taxes and spending “should never be more than necessary to meet the government’s constitutional obligations.” She described herself as pro-freedom, pro-life, pro-Second Amendment, pro-family, and an advocate for fiscal responsibility, and a staunch supporter of the Republican Party platform.

positions.topic: Budget, schools and economy
positions.text: Wrote that Wyoming did not face a budget-funding crisis but “over-taxation and excessive spending,” citing roughly $30 billion in reserves. She argued other Western states were unconstitutionally restricting shipment of Wyoming coal and that the state should reduce regulatory burdens, lower taxes, and protect property rights. On school finance she said she did not believe Wyoming had a funding crisis and that the state should focus on wiser spending and better allocation rather than cuts or new revenue.

positions.topic: Role of government
positions.text: Said a legislator’s role is to protect rights and liberties, defend the Constitution, and keep government limited and accountable, including life, property rights, free speech, and the right to bear arms, and to defend state sovereignty against federal overreach. She said she supported 2023 House Bill 212 to create standing committees reviewing the constitutionality of federal actions.
